title: I made a lateral thinking mystery game with an LLM host (tech demo)
author: whoji
selftext:
Hi all. I'm an LLM hobbyist, and I make small games on the side to try out new models. This one is a tech demo, not a commercial game, but it is fully playable and free in the browser:


https://soup.tier9.games

**What it is**

A lateral thinking puzzle game ("situation puzzles"). You get a short, strange story, like "every morning a boy on an empty island waved at the ferry captain, and one morning he was gone, so the captain turned the ferry around and refused to sail again". You ask yes/no questions. Good questions unlock clues on a mind map. When you think you know the truth, you write your theory and get a score.

**The AI part**

The host runs on Jev, a model that does not generate text at all. It only answers typed questions with probabilities. For each player question I send one request that asks:

- Is this question YES / NO / IRRELEVANT / not a yes-or-no question?
- For every hidden clue: did this question reach it? (a true/false probability)
- Is the player trying to guess the full answer?

The host's lines are hand-written, so the model never writes text. Players can't get it to spoil the answer, and there is nothing to jailbreak into a long rant. It's also fast (about 0.3 to 0.4 s) and cheap: about $0.00014 per question in my tests.

**Things I learned**

- **Wording the clue conditions is the real game design.** If they are too strict, players ask a good question and nothing happens, which feels bad. If they are too loose, one question opens half the map. Example: "is the boy a ghost?" used to unlock 4 clues at once, because the model said yes to two clues and each one also pulled its parent clues in. Now one question can unlock at most one clue, and clues that connect to what you already found go first. A small rule in code fixed it; no prompt change needed.
- **Follow-up questions need history.** Players ask "was it on purpose?" and "it" means something from 3 questions ago. So I send the last few question/answer pairs with every request. Without that, the host feels dumb very fast.
- **Keep the rules in code, not in the prompt.** The model gives probabilities, and code decides with thresholds. When something feels off, I change a number in a JSON file instead of rewriting a prompt and hoping.
- **Test against the real model.** Each story has a list of test questions with expected results. I run them after changing prompts. It costs a few cents and catches problems before players do.
- **Have an offline fallback.** With no API key it switches to a keyword judge. It's worse, but the game never hard-fails, and it's great for testing the UI.

[AI disclosure: I vibe coded most part of the game. The scene art was made with Gemini, a few of the cases were first drafted by me in Chinese (English is my second language) and iterated with an LLM into English, and I used Claude Code a lot for the code.]

**Cost**, if you are wondering: hosting is Cloudflare Pages (free at my size). The model costs roughly $0.006 per monthly player. 1,000 monthly players would be about $6/month.

Feedback very welcome. Thanks!
